2009A16.goal: Consecutive gaps $|a-b|=2$, $|b-c|=3$, $|c-d|=4$; we want the sum of all possible $|a-d|$. Each gap can point either way, so $a-d=\pm2\pm3\pm4$.

tools.name: Absolute values as signs
tools.why: Each difference has two possible signs.

2009A16.approach: List the absolute values of $\pm2\pm3\pm4$. Sign patterns come in opposite pairs with the same absolute value, so four values remain.

steps.title: List values
steps.explain: $2+3+4=9$, $2+3-4=1$, $2-3+4=3$, $-2+3+4=5$. Flipping all signs gives the same absolute values.

2009A16.bridge: Write $a-d$ as a signed sum and list absolute values.
2009A16.shortcut: Fix the sign of one term (say $+4$) and vary the others: $4\pm3\pm2$.
2009A16.recognize: Chains of absolute differences: telescope into a signed sum.

2009A17.goal: Rectangle $ABCD$ ($4\times3$) sits inside right triangle $DEF$ with $A$ on $DE$, $C$ on $DF$ and $EF\perp DB$ at $B$. We want $EF$. Since the angle at $D$ is the rectangle's right angle, $DB$ is the altitude to the hypotenuse.
2009A17.approach: $DB=5$. In right triangle $DBE$, $\angle EDB=\angle ADB$ with $\tan=\tfrac43$; in $DBF$, $\angle BDF=\angle BDC$ with $\tan=\tfrac34$. Add $EB+BF$.

check.q: In a $4\times3$ rectangle with $AB=4$, $AD=3$, what is $\tan\angle ADB$?

2009A17.bridge: Use $DB=5$ and the tangents of the angles at $D$.
traps: Assuming $EF$ is parallel to a side.
2009A17.recognize: A right triangle with its altitude to the hypotenuse: the altitude splits it into similar triangles; tangents of the angles give the pieces.

2009A18.goal: $60\%$ play soccer, $30\%$ swim, and $40\%$ of soccer players swim. We want the percent of non-swimmers who play soccer. Use $100$ children.
2009A18.approach: Soccer $60$, of whom $24$ swim, so $36$ do not. Non-swimmers total $70$. Answer $\tfrac{36}{70}$.

steps.title: Counts
steps.explain: Soccer and swim: $0.4\cdot60=24$. Soccer, no swim: $36$. Non-swimmers: $70$.

2009A18.bridge: Count with $100$ children and divide by the non-swimmers.
solution: Of $100$ children: $60$ soccer, $24$ of them swim.
$36$ soccer players do not swim; $70$ children do not swim.
2009A18.shortcut: Always identify the base of a conditional percent.
2009A18.recognize: "What percent of group X": counts over the size of group X.

2009A19.goal: Circle $B$ (integer radius $r<100$) rolls once around inside circle $A$ (radius $100$) and ends touching at the same points on both circles. We count possible $r$. The point of $B$ in contact returns exactly when $B$'s circumference divides $A$'s.

tools.name: Divisors
tools.why: $2\pi\cdot100$ must be a whole number of $2\pi r$.

2009A19.approach: After one trip, $2\pi\cdot100$ of $B$'s boundary has touched $A$. To touch with the same point of $B$, this must be a whole number of $B$'s circumferences: $r\mid100$.

check.q: How many positive divisors does $100$ have?

2009A19.bridge: Require $100/r$ to be an integer and count divisors.
solution: The contact length $200\pi$ must be a multiple of $2\pi r$, so $r\mid100$.
2009A19.recognize: Rolling-circle returns: arc lengths must match up, giving a divisibility condition.

2009A20.goal: Two cyclists close a $20$ km gap at $1$ km/min, Andrea three times as fast as Lauren. After $5$ minutes Andrea stops. We want when Lauren arrives. Find each speed first.

tools.name: Distance = rate × time
tools.why: For Lauren alone after the stop.

2009A20.approach: $v_L=\tfrac14$ km/min. After $5$ minutes the gap is $15$ km, which Lauren covers alone in $60$ minutes.

steps.title: Remaining time
steps.explain: After $5$ minutes: $15$ km left; Lauren takes $\tfrac{15}{1/4}=60$ minutes. Total $65$.

2009A20.bridge: Find the speeds, the remaining gap, and Lauren's solo time.
solution: After $5$ min the gap is $15$ km.
2009A20.shortcut: Closing speed drops from $1$ to $\tfrac14$ when Andrea stops.
traps: Using Andrea's speed after she stops.
2009A20.recognize: Approach problems: closing speed is the sum; when one stops, only the other's speed counts.

2009A21.goal: Four congruent circles in a ring, each touching its neighbours and the big circle. We want (total small area) / (big area). The small centres form a square.

tools.name: Big radius
tools.why: Distance to a small centre plus its radius.

steps.title: Big radius
steps.explain: Centres are $r\sqrt2$ from the middle; add $r$: $R=r(1+\sqrt2)$.

check.q: For a square of side $2$, how far is a corner from the centre?

2009A21.bridge: Find $R$ in terms of $r$ and compute $\tfrac{4r^2}{R^2}$.
solution: Small centres form a square of side $2r$; $R=r(1+\sqrt2)$.
2009A21.recognize: Rings of tangent circles: centres form a regular polygon; the big radius is the circumradius plus $r$.

2009A22.goal: The twelve numbers ($1$–$6$ twice) are randomly placed on two dice, which are rolled. We want $P(\text{sum}=7)$. Think about which two tiles land on top.

tools.name: Symmetry
tools.fact: \text{the two top tiles are a uniformly random pair of distinct tiles}
tools.why: Random placement and fair rolls make every tile equally likely on top, and the second die's top is one of the other $11$.

2009A22.approach: Whatever tile is on top of the first die (value $v$), the second die's top is a random one of the remaining $11$ tiles. Exactly $2$ of them have value $7-v$.

steps.title: Reduce
steps.explain: The top of die $1$ is some tile with value $v$. The top of die $2$ is equally likely to be any of the other $11$ tiles.

check.q: How many tiles show $7-v$ among the remaining $11$?
check.why: Both copies are still there since $7-v\ne v$.

2009A22.bridge: Condition on the first top tile; the second is random among the other $11$.
solution: The two top tiles are a random pair of distinct tiles from the $12$.
Given the first has value $v$, exactly $2$ of the other $11$ have value $7-v$.
2009A22.shortcut: Ignore the dice entirely: draw two tiles from a bag of twelve.
traps: Thinking the two dice could show the same tile.
2009A22.recognize: Random relabelling plus random rolls: reduce to drawing tiles without replacement.

2009A23.goal: In convex $ABCD$, $AB=9$, $CD=12$, $AC=14$, and $[AED]=[BEC]$. We want $AE$. Equal areas force $AB\parallel CD$, giving similar triangles.

tools.name: Equal areas on a common base
tools.why: $C$ and $D$ are the same distance from line $AB$.

2009A23.approach: Add $[ABE]$ to both equal areas to get $[ABD]=[ABC]$, so $CD\parallel AB$. Then $\triangle ABE\sim\triangle CDE$ with ratio $9:12=3:4$, splitting $AC=14$ into $6$ and $8$.

steps.title: Parallel sides
steps.explain: $[ABD]=[ABE]+[AED]=[ABE]+[BEC]=[ABC]$. Same base $AB$, equal areas: $C$ and $D$ are equally far from $AB$, so $CD\parallel AB$.

check.q: Two triangles share base $AB$ and have equal areas. What can you say about their third vertices?
Split $14$ in ratio $3:4$; the first part is?

2009A23.bridge: Turn the equal areas into $AB\parallel CD$, then use similar triangles.
2009A23.shortcut: Equal "side" triangles at the diagonal intersection always mean a trapezoid.
2009A23.recognize: Equal areas of opposite triangles at a diagonal intersection: the quadrilateral is a trapezoid.

2009A24.goal: Three random vertices of a cube determine a plane. We want the probability that plane passes through the cube's interior. It fails exactly when all three vertices lie on one face.

tools.name: Triples on a face
tools.why: Each face has $4$ vertices; no triple lies on two faces.

2009A24.approach: If the three vertices lie on one face, the plane is that face (no interior points). Otherwise the plane cuts through the cube. Count the face triples and take the complement.

steps.title: Face triples
steps.explain: Each face gives $\binom43=4$ triples; $6$ faces give $24$.

check.q: How many triples of vertices lie on one square face?

2009A24.bridge: Subtract face triples from all triples.
solution: $24$ lie on a face and give face planes.
The other $32$ planes cut the interior: $\tfrac47$.
2009A24.shortcut: Only face planes avoid the interior; every other plane through three vertices slices it.
traps: Thinking corner-cutting planes miss the interior.
2009A24.recognize: Planes through vertices of a polyhedron: the ones that don't enter the interior are exactly the face planes.

2009A25.goal: $I_k=10^{k+2}+64$. We want the most factors of $2$ it can have. Compare the powers of $2$ in the two terms.

tools.name: Power of 2 in a sum
tools.why: Factor out the smaller power; the rest is odd + even.

2009A25.bridge: Compare $k+2$ with $6$; the equal case gives an extra factor of $2$.
2009A25.shortcut: $5^{\text{even}}+1\equiv2\pmod4$, so equal powers add exactly one more $2$.
2009A25.recognize: Powers of $2$ in sums: they equal the smaller power unless the two powers match.
